steps: Transpose swaps rows and columns: a 2×3 becomes 3×2.
Row 1 of A becomes column 1 of \(A^T\).

traps.why: Transposing is not reversing each row — entry (i,j) moves to (j,i), changing the SHAPE from 2×3 to 3×2.
Only symmetric matrices equal their transpose — this one is not even square.

q: Compute \(\det\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 & -3 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ -3 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\) by cofactor expansion along the second row.
steps: Row 2 has only one nonzero entry (\(2\)), so one cofactor survives.

traps.why: The (2,2) cofactor sign is (−1)^{2+2} = +. The checkerboard starts with + at (1,1).
The 2×2 minor still uses ad − bc, with the subtraction.

q: A is a \(2\times 2\) matrix with \(\det A = -4\). Find \(\det(2A)\).
steps: Scaling an \(n\times n\) matrix scales the determinant by \(k^n\): every ROW gets multiplied.

traps.why: kA multiplies BOTH rows by k, and each row multiplication scales det by k — so k² total for 2×2.
Determinants are not scale-invariant — only row REPLACEMENT operations leave det unchanged.

steps: Two vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) are dependent exactly when one is a multiple of the other — equivalently \(\det\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ -1 & -3\end{bmatrix} = 0\).

traps.why: Test with the determinant (or look for a scalar multiple): zero ⇒ dependent, nonzero ⇒ independent.

traps.ans: Cannot be determined without a third vector
traps.why: Independence of TWO vectors is decidable on its own — a multiple relationship either exists or it does not.

q: A \(2\times 2\) matrix has eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 = -1\) and \(\lambda_2 = 1\). Find \(\det A\) and \(\text{tr}\,A\).
steps: The determinant is the PRODUCT of the eigenvalues: \(-1\cdot1 = -1\).

traps.why: Swapped: det = product, trace = sum — they are the constant and (negated) linear coefficients of the characteristic polynomial.

traps.ans: Cannot be found without the matrix itself
traps.why: det and trace are determined BY the eigenvalues — that is exactly what the characteristic polynomial encodes.
